summary: Proposes a simple file format for storing black-and-white bitmaps, with a short header giving the width and number of lines. It was meant for short-term storage and passing data between closely coupled programs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 797 proposes a file format for simple bitmaps with one bit per pixel. A 10-octet header describes the image dimensions and increments, followed by the pixel data.

questions: simple one bit per pixel file format
how to store black and white images
what is the rfc 797 bitmap file format
subtitle: A simple file layout for storing one-bit-per-pixel bitmap images.

tldr.problem: Programs need a simple way to store and pass bitmaps with one bit per pixel.
tldr.mechanism: The format stores width, height, and x and y increments in a 10-octet header, followed by image bits packed in scan-line order.
tldr.outcome: The author proposes the format for short-term storage and transfer between closely coupled programs.

today: RFC 797 proposes a simple bitmap file format for short-term storage and data exchange between closely coupled programs. It describes the format and example increment values.

sections.title: Purpose and File Layout
sections.content:
The memo proposes a format for storing simple bitmaps in files. It is intended for short-term storage and passing data between closely coupled programs, and the file stores data in 8-bit octets.

The format begins with ten octets of header followed by the bitmap itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is for programs that need to store and pass a simple bitmap. The header comes first, followed by the image data.

sections.title: Header and Pixel Order
sections.content:
The first four octets give the width of each line, the next four give the number of lines, and the next two give the x and y increments. The width and length fields are stored with the most significant octet first.

Each line is scanned left to right, and lines start at the top and continue down. Each line ends on an octet boundary; unused bits at the end are zero-filled.
sections.plainLanguage: The header tells a reader how wide and tall the bitmap is and gives its x and y increments. Pixel data is arranged across each line, then down the image.

sections.title: Increment Values for Facsimile Data
sections.content:
The x and y increments specify how much space lies between pixels. For an ordinary display, both are one.

The RFC gives Rapicom 450 examples: Fine Detail uses increments of one and one, Quality uses one and two, and Express uses one and three. When displayed, each scan line is repeated according to the y increment.
sections.plainLanguage: The increment values describe spacing and can also tell a display how often to repeat a scan line. The memo gives settings for three Rapicom 450 modes.
